comparativeCohorts.group: Overdose, toxic exposure and clinical access
comparativeCohorts.judgment: Naloxone/MOUD, HIV linkage and poison triage offer severe-harm pathways with recognizable clinical endpoints. Broad providers/peer portfolios remain credible alternatives but cash gifts may substitute reimbursement or buy less directly observable participation. Lahai and CLR merit promotion if additional treatment capacity and full donated-resource costs are stronger; no price ranking claimed.

NoHLA/Children’s Alliance can affect statewide coverage/workforce rules; WithinReach adds an observable enrollment/vaccine completion comparator. WAA’s current backlog, intervention mix and targeted benefits make it a useful later comparator; refugee and general navigation portfolios dilute the directly modeled health pathway. Scale is high for policy but implementation and coalition credit are weaker than clinical evidence.

Prioritize distinctive severe detention-health, statewide income and implemented land-use hypotheses. NJP is a strong direct-case alternative to CLS; both would need full case costs and changes in actual access. Sightline/Sage overlap Futurewise’s housing pathway; policy research publication alone is weaker implementation evidence. WHAEN remains plausible but its current split makes the original broad advocacy claim insufficient for its selected slot.

DRCC’s geographically concentrated exposure and concrete filter/permit work are more tractable than general organizing. TFF’s source-control product pathway can scale statewide, with latency and substitution risks. Front and Centered shares the Ash Grove case and cannot independently claim the same harm avoided; ecological and waste outputs require especially uncertain human-health transfer.

Population street design/transit changes have larger plausible reach than bike distributions/recreation, but public capital opportunity cost and actual crash/activity changes can reverse the ranking. Feet First is a credible substitute for Streets Alliance if actual infrastructure contribution is stronger. Publicly funded school cycling and retail/recreation need incremental-use rather than participant counts.

Protection-order implementation and high-risk de-escalation target severe injury; KCSARC provides a specialist trauma endpoint, ADWAS a distinct accessibility gap, and LifeWire a housing/safety comparator. CHOOSE180’s lower recidivism remains selection-prone. Other survivor agencies are not judged ineffective; add them if marginal completed treatment/safety evidence beats chosen comparators. All safety policies require autonomy/equity and unintended-harm checks.

Specific accessibility repairs/falls prevention offer durable functioning pathways, although two repair organizations plus two broad senior portfolios create overlap risk. Separate county intake and independent recipients justify comparison. Full labor, capital, volunteer and public subsidy costs are needed; utility/housing assistance may outperform if they address actual acute health bottlenecks.

comparativeCohorts.group: Youth, developmental disability and basic needs
comparativeCohorts.judgment: All retain credible deprivation/access mechanisms. Current service volume is not a causal effect; disability gains may overlap statutory entitlement, shelter nights may substitute other providers, and food tonnage is not nutrition improvement. They are lower first-pass research priority because incremental unrestricted-gift-to-health chains are broader, not because their beneficiaries are less valuable. Kindering remains a named alternate and Mary’s Place prevention research may improve future tractability.
